conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: If laparoscopic cholecystectomy cannot be carried out within 1 week of diagnosis, it is delayed until more than 4 weeks after diagnosis, once the acute episode has subsided (NICE).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which of the following is a complication of acute cholecystitis arising within the gallbladder itself?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Perforation leading to peritonitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Within-gallbladder complications include empyema, mucocele, gangrenous GB, perforation → peritonitis, and chronic GB carcinoma. Cholangitis, pancreatitis, gallstone ileus and Mirizzi's are ductal/beyond complications.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is a gallbladder mucocele?
options: A stone eroding into the duodenum
Malignant transformation of the gallbladder mucosa
Mucus secretion from an obstructed gallbladder
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Mucus secretion from an obstructed gallbladder
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A mucocele is mucus secretion from an obstructed gallbladder, distinct from an empyema (pus).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with acute cholecystitis develops jaundice; imaging shows a cystic-duct stone compressing the common hepatic duct. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Mirizzi's syndrome
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Mirizzi's syndrome is a cystic-duct stone compressing the common hepatic duct, producing obstructive jaundice.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How does gallstone ileus arise as a complication?
options: A stone impacts at the ampulla of Vater, obstructing pancreatic outflow
Ascending gut organisms infect the common bile duct
Mucus accumulates in an obstructed gallbladder
A cystic-duct stone compresses the common hepatic duct
A cholecystoduodenal fistula allows a stone into the terminal ileum, causing SBO
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: A cholecystoduodenal fistula allows a stone into the terminal ileum, causing SBO
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Gallstone ileus results from a cholecystoduodenal fistula → stone in the terminal ileum → small bowel obstruction.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A septic patient with acute cholecystitis is found to have a pus-filled gallbladder. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Gangrenous GB — antibiotics alone, no intervention required
GB empyema — IV antibiotics plus cholecystostomy or cholecystectomy
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: GB empyema — IV antibiotics plus cholecystostomy or cholecystectomy
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: GB empyema is a pus-filled gallbladder, managed with IV antibiotics plus cholecystostomy or cholecystectomy.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which tool is used to assess sepsis risk in an adult with acute cholecystitis in hospital?
options: Courvoisier's law applied at the bedside
qSOFA — respiratory rate, GCS and systolic blood pressure
NEWS2 — the national early warning score
The Rockall score for risk stratification
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: NEWS2 — the national early warning score
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: NEWS2 is the tool used to assess risk of severe illness or death from sepsis in anyone aged 16 or over in an acute hospital setting (NICE), with escalation and antibiotic timing keyed to the score. qSOFA is a research construct and is not the UK ward screening tool.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the core pathological process of acute pancreatitis?
options: Ischaemic infarction of the pancreatic head
Autoimmune destruction of the islets of Langerhans
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Enzyme-mediated autodigestion leading to necrosis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas by enzyme-mediated autodigestion leading to necrosis, most commonly caused by gallstones and alcohol.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which two causes account for the majority of acute pancreatitis cases?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Gallstones and alcohol
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Within the 'I GET SMASHED' aetiology, gallstones and ethanol dominate as the commonest causes.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which of the following is an iatrogenic cause of acute pancreatitis within the 'I GET SMASHED' mnemonic?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ERCP
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP is the iatrogenic cause within I GET SMASHED.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which drug is recognised as a cause of acute pancreatitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Azathioprine
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Recognised drug causes include azathioprine, furosemide, valproate, mesalazine and bendroflumethiazide.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the final common pathway underlying acute pancreatitis?
options: Direct bacterial invasion of acinar cells
Reduced perfusion → ischaemia → infarction without any enzyme activation
Raised intracellular Ca²⁺ → premature trypsinogen activation → trypsin → autodigestion
Raised ductal pressure → bile reflux → cholangitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Raised intracellular Ca²⁺ → premature trypsinogen activation → trypsin → autodigestion
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The final common pathway is raised intracellular Ca²⁺ → premature trypsinogen activation → trypsin → autodigestion → acinar cell necrosis → inflammatory cascade → (severe) multi-organ failure.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: In gallstone pancreatitis, where does the stone act to trigger the disease?
options: At the common hepatic duct, compressing it externally
In the terminal ileum via a fistula
At the sphincter of Oddi, causing obstruction and back-pressure
In the cystic duct, causing gallbladder distension
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: At the sphincter of Oddi, causing obstruction and back-pressure
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The gallstone mechanism is a stone at the sphincter of Oddi → obstruction → back-pressure, triggering the same trypsin activation cascade.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis develops hypocalcaemia. What is the mechanism?
options: Renal calcium wasting from the associated acute kidney injury
Fat necrosis releases free fatty acids that bind serum calcium (saponification)
Dilution from the sheer volume of crystalloid given in resuscitation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Fat necrosis releases free fatty acids that bind serum calcium (saponification)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Circulating enzymes cause fat necrosis; the free fatty acids bind serum Ca²⁺, causing hypocalcaemia by saponification.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. What anatomical feature of the pancreas explains the back radiation?
options: The pancreas is supplied by the phrenic nerve
The pancreas shares innervation with the diaphragm
The pancreas lies within the lesser sac only
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: The pancreas is retroperitoneal
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The pain radiates to the back because the pancreas is retroperitoneal — the anatomical reason for back radiation.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis is noted to have periumbilical bruising (Cullen's sign) and flank bruising (Grey-Turner's sign). What do these indicate?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey-Turner's sign (flank bruising) both indicate retroperitoneal haemorrhage in severe necrotising disease.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why is lipase preferred over amylase for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
options: It is cheaper and more widely available
It rises only in gallstone aetiology
It correlates directly with disease severity and predicts organ failure
It is more sensitive/specific and has a longer half-life (better >24 h after onset)
It is unaffected by renal impairment
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It is more sensitive/specific and has a longer half-life (better >24 h after onset)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase with a longer half-life, making it better beyond 24 h after onset. Amylase falls quickly after onset, so a normal amylase does not exclude the diagnosis, and it does NOT correlate with severity.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What enzyme threshold is diagnostic of acute pancreatitis?
options: Amylase or lipase greater than 3× the upper limit of normal
Lipase greater than 2× the upper limit of normal
Amylase greater than 10× the upper limit of normal only
Amylase greater than 1.5× the upper limit of normal
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Amylase or lipase greater than 3× the upper limit of normal
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Both amylase and lipase are diagnostic at >3× the upper limit of normal.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: In a patient with acute pancreatitis, what is the significance of an ALT above 150?
options: It points strongly to a gallstone aetiology
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It points strongly to a gallstone aetiology
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A raised ALT, particularly above 150, points strongly to a gallstone aetiology — the LFT clue to the cause. It says nothing about severity and does not confirm alcohol.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: When is contrast-enhanced CT best timed in acute pancreatitis, and why?
options: Within 24 hours of admission, to grade disease severity
At 6–10 days, because imaging too early misses necrosis
At 4 weeks, once a pseudocyst forms
On admission, to confirm the diagnosis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: At 6–10 days, because imaging too early misses necrosis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is best at 6–10 days to show oedema/necrosis; too early misses necrosis. It is used in persistent inflammation or organ failure.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the 'sentinel loop sign' seen on abdominal X-ray in acute pancreatitis?
options: A dilated bowel loop adjacent to the pancreas
Multiple air-fluid levels throughout the abdomen
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: A dilated bowel loop adjacent to the pancreas
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The sentinel loop sign is a dilated bowel loop adjacent to the pancreas (AXR is not routine).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Using the Glasgow score, which result indicates severe acute pancreatitis?
options: A score of ≥3, assessed in the first 48 hours
Any score assessed on admission only
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: A score of ≥3, assessed in the first 48 hours
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The Glasgow score is assessed in the first 48 hours and is a binary predictor: ≥3 predicts severe disease and <3 predicts a mild course — there is no "moderate" band. CRP >150 at 48 h is also used. Severity itself is defined by organ failure, not by points.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which of the following is a criterion in the Glasgow (PANCREAS) severity score?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Calcium <2 mmol/L
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: PANCREAS criteria include PaO₂ <8 kPa, Age >55, Neutrophils >15, Calcium <2 mmol/L, Renal urea >16, Enzymes (LDH >600 or AST >200), Albumin <32, and Sugar >10 mmol/L.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis requires fluid resuscitation. What is the recommended urine output target?
options: No target is needed if BP is normal
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: >0.5 mL/kg/h
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Goal-directed IV fluid resuscitation with a balanced crystalloid is titrated to clinical response and a urine output of >0.5 mL/kg/h, avoiding fluid overload.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why is morphine traditionally avoided for analgesia in acute pancreatitis?
options: It raises sphincter of Oddi pressure
It is ineffective for visceral pain
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It raises sphincter of Oddi pressure
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Morphine is traditionally avoided because it raises sphincter of Oddi pressure; other IV opioids are used instead.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the recommended nutritional approach in severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis?
options: Enteral nutrition within 72 h; do not keep NBM without a clear reason
Strict NBM for at least 7 days in all patients regardless of severity
Oral intake only when amylase normalises
No nutrition until CT confirms resolution
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Enteral nutrition within 72 h; do not keep NBM without a clear reason
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Enteral nutrition should be started within 72 hours of presentation in severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis (NICE), with parenteral nutrition only if enteral fails or is contraindicated. Patients should not be made NBM unless there is a clear reason such as vomiting.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: According to NICE, what is the antibiotic policy in acute pancreatitis?
options: No prophylactic antibiotics; antibiotics only for confirmed infected necrosis
Prophylactic antibiotics for all patients on admission
Antibiotics only once a pseudocyst forms
Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics in all predicted-severe cases
Oral antibiotics for all gallstone aetiology
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: No prophylactic antibiotics; antibiotics only for confirmed infected necrosis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: NICE advises no prophylactic antimicrobials in acute pancreatitis. Antibiotics are reserved for confirmed infected necrosis, guided by culture and local policy.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient has biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis. Which procedure is indicated?
options: Early ERCP + sphincterotomy for urgent biliary decompression
Elective cholecystectomy deferred by several months
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Early ERCP + sphincterotomy for urgent biliary decompression
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Early ERCP + sphincterotomy is indicated for biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis, where the duct needs urgent decompression, or for persistent CBD obstruction. Predicted-severe disease alone is not an indication.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Six weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis, a patient has a retrogastric fluid collection with enzymes in a fibrous wall that has no epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pancreatic pseudocyst
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A pseudocyst occurs >4 weeks after onset: fluid + enzymes in a fibrous wall with no epithelium (hence 'pseudo'), classically retrogastric.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How is a pancreatic pseudocyst managed?
options: Immediate surgical excision in every case as soon as it is detected
Observe — many resolve; cystogastrostomy if symptomatic or persistent
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Observe — many resolve; cystogastrostomy if symptomatic or persistent
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Most pseudocysts are managed conservatively as many resolve. Intervention (endoscopic cystogastrostomy) is reserved for those that are symptomatic, enlarging, infected, or causing gastric outlet or biliary obstruction.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with acute pancreatitis has a peripancreatic fluid collection with no wall on imaging. What is the appropriate management principle?
options: Aspirate the collection immediately to confirm it is sterile
Avoid aspiration, as it precipitates infection; it mostly resolves
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Avoid aspiration, as it precipitates infection; it mostly resolves
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A peripancreatic fluid collection is early with no wall and mostly resolves; aspiration should be avoided as it precipitates infection.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with acute pancreatitis deteriorates at three weeks with fever, a raised WCC and gas within a necrotic collection on CT. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Infected pancreatic necrosis — antibiotics and step-up drainage
Walled-off necrosis, uninfected — continue supportive care
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Infected pancreatic necrosis — antibiotics and step-up drainage
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Fever, a raised WCC and gas within a necrotic collection indicate infected pancreatic necrosis, managed with antibiotics guided by culture and a step-up approach to drainage, escalating to necrosectomy if needed.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis develops respiratory failure with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. What is the mechanism and management?
options: ARDS — systemic cytokines cause leaky pulmonary capillaries; ITU-level respiratory support
Pulmonary embolism from a DVT; treat with thrombolysis
Pleural effusion alone; treat with a chest drain
Pneumonia from direct bacterial seeding of the lung; treat with oral antibiotics
Pulmonary oedema from left heart failure; treat with diuretics
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ARDS — systemic cytokines cause leaky pulmonary capillaries; ITU-level respiratory support
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ARDS arises from systemic cytokines causing leaky pulmonary capillaries, and is managed with ITU-level respiratory support.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient develops hyperglycaemia following severe acute pancreatitis. What is the mechanism and management?
options: Islet of Langerhans destruction — insulin infusion
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Islet of Langerhans destruction — insulin infusion
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Hyperglycaemia results from islet of Langerhans destruction and is managed with an insulin infusion.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the predominant histological type of cholangiocarcinoma?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Adenocarcinoma
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the biliary tree, with 95% being adenocarcinomas; it is generally silent until late and most are inoperable at diagnosis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A cholangiocarcinoma is located at the bifurcation of the left and right hepatic ducts. What is this tumour called, and how common is this site?
options: Distal common bile duct tumour — the commonest site
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Klatskin (perihilar) tumour — the commonest site
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A perihilar tumour at the bifurcation of the left + right hepatic ducts is a Klatskin tumour, and it is the commonest site.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What unifying mechanism links the major risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma?
options: Acute biliary obstruction with secondary infection
Chronic biliary inflammation leading to malignant transformation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Chronic biliary inflammation leading to malignant transformation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The unifying theme is chronic biliary inflammation → malignant transformation; PSC, liver flukes and congenital duct dilation all funnel through this mechanism.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the main risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: PSC is the main risk factor, causing chronic ductal scarring and inflammation.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with ulcerative colitis is at increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Through which intermediate condition is this link best explained?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: UC is strongly linked to cholangiocarcinoma via PSC (UC → PSC → cholangiocarcinoma).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient from SE Asia is diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma. Which risk factor best explains the higher incidence in this region?
options: Liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Liver flukes (e.g. Clonorchis sinensis) explain the increased incidence of cholangiocarcinoma in SE Asia.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which congenital condition involving intrahepatic duct dilation is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Caroli's disease
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Caroli's disease is intrahepatic duct dilation; a choledochal cyst is bile duct dilation. Both are congenital risk factors.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: An elderly patient presents with painless jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools and steatorrhoea, having been previously well. Which feature of the presentation is most characteristic of cholangiocarcinoma?
options: Sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back
Acute colicky pain relieved by vomiting
Painless obstructive jaundice that is generally silent until late
Fever with rigors as the first symptom
Early severe weight loss occurring long before any jaundice
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Painless obstructive jaundice that is generally silent until late
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma is generally asymptomatic until late, then presents with painless obstructive jaundice plus pruritus, dark urine, pale stools and steatorrhoea.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: On examination a patient has a palpable gallbladder with painless jaundice. By Courvoisier's law, what does this suggest?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Cancer, not stones
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Courvoisier's law: a palpable GB + painless jaundice points to cancer (e.g. cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic head), not stones.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with cholangiocarcinoma is found to have a palpable left supraclavicular lymph node. What is this sign called?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Troisier's sign (Virchow's node)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node) is Troisier's sign, indicating GI malignancy.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A periumbilical nodule is found in a patient with cholangiocarcinoma. What does this represent?
options: Sister Mary Joseph nodule — intra-abdominal spread
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Sister Mary Joseph nodule — intra-abdominal spread
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical metastatic tumour deposit indicating intra-abdominal spread. It is a nodule, not a lymph node.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How is the diagnosis of cholangiocarcinoma usually made?
options: A negative ERCP brushing reliably excludes it
On imaging, with tissue obtained only where it changes management
Histology is always required before any surgery can proceed
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: On imaging, with tissue obtained only where it changes management
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Diagnosis is usually made on imaging. Tissue is obtained where it changes management, such as before palliative chemotherapy — but ERCP brushings are insensitive, so a negative result does not exclude cancer, and a resectable tumour may go to surgery on imaging alone.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which tumour marker is used in cholangiocarcinoma, and what are its limits?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: CA19-9 is the biliary tumour marker (CEA may also be raised), alongside obstructive LFTs. It supports rather than makes the diagnosis — benign biliary obstruction and cholangitis also raise it.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which liver function pattern is expected in cholangiocarcinoma?
options: Obstructive LFTs: raised bilirubin, ALP and GGT
Normal LFTs with a raised amylase
Raised ALT and AST with normal bilirubin
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Obstructive LFTs: raised bilirubin, ALP and GGT
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The LFT pattern is obstructive: raised bilirubin, ALP and GGT.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the staging modality of choice in cholangiocarcinoma?
options: Catheter angiography of the hepatic arteries
CT TAP — assessing metastases and resectability
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: CT TAP — assessing metastases and resectability
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: CT TAP is the staging modality of choice, assessing metastases and resectability.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which investigation in cholangiocarcinoma is therapeutic and can also obtain brushings at the same sitting?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ERCP
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP is a therapeutic procedure — it stents the obstructed duct — and can take brushings at the same time. MRCP is the non-invasive diagnostic equivalent but cannot decompress or sample.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How are the hepatic arteries and portal vein assessed before surgery in cholangiocarcinoma?
options: Initial detection of a dilated biliary tree
On the vascular phases of the staging CT
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: On the vascular phases of the staging CT
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Vascular assessment is done on the arterial and portal phases of the staging CT, which map the hepatic arteries and portal vein.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the only definitive cure for cholangiocarcinoma, and what is the prognostic reality?
options: Liver transplant, which is offered to all patients
Complete surgical resection — but most are inoperable and recurrence is common
ERCP stenting, which removes the tumour
Palliative chemotherapy, which is curative in most patients treated
Radiotherapy alone, with full cure in the majority
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Complete surgical resection — but most are inoperable and recurrence is common
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The only definitive cure is complete surgical resection, but most tumours are inoperable at diagnosis and recurrence is common even after complete resection.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A resectable cholangiocarcinoma is located in the distal common bile duct. Which operation is appropriate?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple's)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Distal common duct tumours are treated with pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple's), with adjuvant chemotherapy after a complete resection.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A resectable intrahepatic/Klatskin (perihilar) cholangiocarcinoma requires which operation?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Partial hepatectomy + biliary tree reconstruction
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Intrahepatic/Klatskin (perihilar) tumours are treated with partial hepatectomy + biliary tree reconstruction; distal tumours get a Whipple's.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with an inoperable cholangiocarcinoma has obstructive jaundice. What is the commonest palliative intervention?
options: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage as first-line
ERCP stenting to relieve the obstructive jaundice
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ERCP stenting to relieve the obstructive jaundice
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP stenting is the commonest palliative act, relieving the obstructive jaundice. If ERCP fails or the tumour cannot be reached endoscopically, percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is used.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: In a patient with cholangiocarcinoma where palliative ERCP stenting fails, what is the next option?
options: Repeat the same stent procedure indefinitely
Surgical bypass, which is now the first choice
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: If ERCP stenting fails or the tumour cannot be reached endoscopically, percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is used; surgical bypass is now rarely needed. Palliative chemotherapy is also an option.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A 42-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe, steady right upper quadrant pain, each settling within hours. She is afebrile, with normal CRP, WCC and LFTs, and Murphy's sign is negative. What is the single best explanation for this presentation?
options: Stone in Hartmann's pouch compressing the common hepatic duct
Sustained cystic duct obstruction with gallbladder wall inflammation
Gallbladder contracting against a stone transiently obstructing the cystic duct
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Gallbladder contracting against a stone transiently obstructing the cystic duct
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Biliary colic is pain from the gallbladder contracting against a stone that transiently obstructs the cystic duct — temporary obstruction with no inflammation, hence no fever, normal markers/LFTs and a negative Murphy's sign. Despite the name, the pain is steady rather than colicky.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which feature best distinguishes ascending cholangitis from acute cholecystitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Presence of jaundice
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Both involve obstruction, inflammation and fever, but ascending cholangitis is at the CBD with infected bile, producing jaundice in addition to fever. Cholecystitis (cystic duct) has fever without jaundice.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What keeps cholesterol soluble within bile?
options: Bile salts and phospholipids forming micelles
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Bile salts and phospholipids forming micelles
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Bile is cholesterol + phospholipids + bile pigments. Cholesterol is kept soluble by bile salts and phospholipids forming micelles; tipping this balance causes cholesterol to precipitate into stones.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A 28-year-old man with hereditary spherocytosis develops gallstones. Which stone type is most likely, and why?
options: Cholesterol stones, due to excess cholesterol secretion into the bile
Mixed stones, due to gallbladder stasis
Pigment stones, due to oestrogen excess
Cholesterol stones, due to a deficiency of bile salts in bile
Pigment stones, due to chronic haemolysis producing excess unconjugated bilirubin
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pigment stones, due to chronic haemolysis producing excess unconjugated bilirubin
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Pigment stones (bilirubin polymers + calcium bilirubinate) are driven by chronic haemolysis such as sickle cell or spherocytosis, which generates excess unconjugated bilirubin and leads to pigment stone formation.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Cholesterol gallstones are most strongly driven by which of the following?
options: Excess cholesterol or bile-salt deficiency with gallbladder stasis
Chronic haemolysis producing excess unconjugated bilirubin
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Excess cholesterol or bile-salt deficiency with gallbladder stasis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Cholesterol stones are predominantly cholesterol, driven by excess cholesterol or bile-salt deficiency plus gallbladder stasis/reduced motility. Haemolysis and duct strictures drive pigment stones.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient who had a terminal ileal resection for Crohn's disease develops gallstones. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Rapid weight loss increases biliary cholesterol saturation markedly
Bile salts are not reabsorbed at the terminal ileum, causing bile-salt deficiency
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Bile salts are not reabsorbed at the terminal ileum, causing bile-salt deficiency
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: In Crohn's/ileal resection, bile salts are not reabsorbed at the terminal ileum, producing bile-salt deficiency and predisposing to cholesterol stones.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How do pregnancy and the oral contraceptive pill increase the risk of gallstones?
options: They increase gallbladder contractility via raised CCK
They reduce bile-salt reabsorption at the ileum
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Oestrogen increases biliary cholesterol secretion
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Pregnancy and the OCP raise gallstone risk because oestrogen increases biliary cholesterol secretion, favouring cholesterol stone formation.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why does biliary colic pain characteristically radiate to the right shoulder or subscapular region?
options: Direct spread through the common bile duct
Irritation of the ampulla of Vater
Compression of the common hepatic duct
Stimulation of CCK receptors in the shoulder
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Referred via the phrenic nerve/diaphragm
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The radiation to the right shoulder/subscapular region is referred pain via the phrenic nerve and diaphragm.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient reports that their RUQ pain is reliably triggered by eating fatty meals. What is the mechanism?
options: Fatty food triggers CCK release, causing gallbladder contraction against the stone
Fatty food precipitates cholesterol crystals acutely within the duct
Fatty food causes ampullary stone impaction
Fatty food directly dilates the common bile duct
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Fatty food triggers CCK release, causing gallbladder contraction against the stone
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Fatty food precipitates pain because fatty acids trigger CCK release, which causes the gallbladder to contract against the stone — the mechanism behind the classic history.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which finding would argue against simple biliary colic and suggest acute cholecystitis instead?
options: Severe RUQ pain settling within a few hours
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: A positive Murphy's sign
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Biliary colic has defining negatives: no fever, normal CRP/WCC, normal LFTs, and no peritonism or Murphy's sign. A positive Murphy's sign points to cholecystitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the first-line investigation in suspected gallstone disease?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Transabdominal ultrasound
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Transabdominal USS is first-line, showing stones/sludge, gallbladder wall thickness and bile duct dilation.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with biliary symptoms has an inconclusive ultrasound and raised LFTs with a dilated duct. What is the most appropriate next imaging step?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: MRCP
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: MRCP is used if USS is inconclusive or to image the CBD when LFTs are raised or the duct is dilated. ERCP follows only if CBD stones need removing.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: During an acute biliary colic attack, which blood test pattern is expected?
options: Normal inflammatory markers and normal LFTs
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Normal inflammatory markers and normal LFTs
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Biliary colic is transient obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone, without inflammation or obstruction of the common bile duct, so LFTs and inflammatory markers are typically normal during as well as between attacks. A raised ALP and bilirubin (obstruction pattern) points to CBD stones; a raised WCC/CRP suggests cholecystitis; a raised amylase suggests pancreatitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the definitive management of symptomatic gallstone disease?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Analgesia (paracetamol ± NSAIDs ± opiates) treats pain, but elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient is found to have CBD stones on pre-operative imaging. How should these be managed in relation to the gallbladder?
options: MRCP will remove the duct stones
Cholecystectomy alone will clear the duct stones
Analgesia until the stones pass spontaneously
Percutaneous cholecystostomy alone, with no further treatment needed
Duct clearance by ERCP or at surgery, plus cholecystectomy for the gallbladder
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Duct clearance by ERCP or at surgery, plus cholecystectomy for the gallbladder
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Both need addressing: the duct is cleared by ERCP before or during cholecystectomy, or surgically at the time of cholecystectomy, and the gallbladder is removed (NICE).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A 55-year-old presents with RUQ pain, fever and jaundice. Which complication of gallstones does this triad represent?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice is Charcot's triad, indicating ascending cholangitis from an infected CBD.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and a markedly raised amylase. Which gallstone complication is most likely?
options: Acute pancreatitis from a stone impacted at the ampulla
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Acute pancreatitis from a stone impacted at the ampulla
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Gallstone pancreatitis occurs when a stone impacts at the ampulla, giving epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised amylase.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient has obstructive jaundice, but imaging shows no stone within the common bile duct itself. A stone is seen in Hartmann's pouch. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Mirizzi syndrome
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Mirizzi syndrome is a stone in Hartmann's pouch compressing the common hepatic duct, causing obstructive jaundice without a CBD stone.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: An elderly, septic patient has gallbladder distension filled with pus on imaging. What is the diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Chronic cholecystitis — elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy once the symptoms have settled
Gallbladder empyema — resuscitation and IV antibiotics, then cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy if unfit
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Gallbladder empyema — resuscitation and IV antibiotics, then cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy if unfit
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Gallbladder empyema is a pus-filled gallbladder in an unwell/septic patient; USS/CT confirms. Management is resuscitation and IV antibiotics with drainage — laparoscopic cholecystectomy, or image-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy if the patient is unfit for surgery, with cholecystectomy later.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: An elderly patient presents with small bowel obstruction. AXR shows pneumobilia, dilated small bowel loops and an ectopic stone. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Gallstone ileus
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Gallstone ileus is a stone impacting the terminal ileum via a cholecystoduodenal fistula, causing SBO. Rigler's triad on AXR = pneumobilia + SBO + ectopic stone.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Bouveret's syndrome and gallstone ileus share the same underlying mechanism. What distinguishes them?
options: Presence versus absence of infected bile
Obstruction of the cystic duct versus the CBD
Cholesterol versus pigment stone composition, which determines where the stone finally lodges
Stone lodging in the proximal duodenum (gastric outflow obstruction) versus the terminal ileum (SBO)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Stone lodging in the proximal duodenum (gastric outflow obstruction) versus the terminal ileum (SBO)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Both arise from the same cholecystoduodenal fistula. A stone in the duodenum causes gastric outflow obstruction (Bouveret's); a stone in the terminal ileum causes SBO (gallstone ileus).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which complication of long-standing gallstones is associated with chronic gallbladder inflammation and carries a poor prognosis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Gallbladder cancer
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Gallbladder cancer is associated with chronic gallstone-related inflammation; it is rare and has a poor prognosis. No causative link has been established (NICE).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: On ultrasound a patient is found to have a small, shrunken gallbladder. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Chronic cholecystitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Chronic cholecystitis is recurrent/untreated inflammation producing a small shrunken gallbladder on USS, managed with elective cholecystectomy.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with known gallstones now has RUQ pain, a positive Murphy's sign, fever and raised WCC/CRP, but no jaundice. What is the most likely complication?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Acute cholecystitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Acute cholecystitis (the commonest complication) is cystic duct + GB wall inflammation: RUQ pain, positive Murphy's, fever and raised WCC/CRP, without the jaundice that defines cholangitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which set of clinical findings correctly matches the 'three presentations' framework for gallstone disease?
options: Colic = + Murphy's; cholecystitis = + Charcot's triad; cholangitis = pain only
Colic = pain + jaundice; cholecystitis = pain only; cholangitis = + Murphy's
All three present identically with fever and jaundice
Colic = + Charcot's triad; cholecystitis = pain only; cholangitis = a positive Murphy's sign
Colic = pain only; cholecystitis = pain + Murphy's + inflammation; cholangitis = + Charcot's triad
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Colic = pain only; cholecystitis = pain + Murphy's + inflammation; cholangitis = + Charcot's triad
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The three presentations: biliary colic = pain only (no fever, normal markers); cholecystitis = pain + Murphy's + inflammation; cholangitis = the above plus Charcot's triad (RUQ pain + fever + jaundice).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Ascending cholangitis is best defined as which of the following?
options: Transient cystic duct obstruction with no inflammation
Inflammation of the gallbladder wall arising from a sustained cystic duct obstruction
Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, requiring both common bile duct obstruction and infection
Compression of the common hepatic duct by a cystic-duct stone
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, requiring both common bile duct obstruction and infection
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Ascending cholangitis is bacterial infection of the biliary tree — the third and most dangerous step of the biliary triad, requiring both obstruction of the common bile duct and infection of the bile behind it. The site (CBD, not cystic duct) is what separates it from cholecystitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why does bacterial colonisation alone rarely cause cholangitis?
options: Bile is bactericidal, so obstruction makes no difference
Infection alone always produces jaundice even without any obstruction
Obstruction is also needed — the 'two-hit requirement' of obstruction + infection
The gallbladder neutralises all colonising organisms
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Obstruction is also needed — the 'two-hit requirement' of obstruction + infection
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Cholangitis requires a two-hit combination of obstruction + infection. Without obstruction, colonisation alone rarely causes cholangitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the commonest causative organism of ascending cholangitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: E. coli
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: E. coli is the commonest organism ('E.scending coli-angitis'), followed by Klebsiella and Enterococcus.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the commonest cause of the biliary obstruction underlying ascending cholangitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Gallstones
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Gallstones are the commonest cause of biliary obstruction. Others include ERCP/instrumentation, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatitis, PSC and parasitic infection.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which is an iatrogenic cause of biliary obstruction leading to cholangitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ERCP / biliary instrumentation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP/biliary instrumentation is the iatrogenic cause of biliary obstruction leading to cholangitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How does biliary obstruction lead to systemic sepsis in ascending cholangitis?
options: Raised intraluminal pressure drives bacteria/toxins back into the bloodstream
Pancreatic enzymes are forced into the portal vein
Bacteria directly digest the bile duct wall releasing endotoxin
Obstruction triggers an autoimmune systemic response
Stasis converts bilirubin into a circulating toxin
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Raised intraluminal pressure drives bacteria/toxins back into the bloodstream
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Biliary stasis + raised intraluminal pressure makes colonisation pathological, and the raised pressure drives bacteria/toxins back into the bloodstream, causing sepsis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A 60-year-old presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice. Which eponymous triad does this represent?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Charcot's triad
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice is Charcot's triad, the classic presentation of ascending cholangitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with known cholangitis becomes hypotensive and confused in addition to having RUQ pain, fever and jaundice. What does this pentad indicate?
options: Cushing's response — raised intracranial pressure with bradycardia
Reynolds' pentad — severe cholangitis with shock, requiring immediate escalation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Reynolds' pentad — severe cholangitis with shock, requiring immediate escalation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Reynolds' pentad is Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion, indicating severe cholangitis with shock — escalate immediately.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which combination of findings makes up the obstructive jaundice picture in cholangitis?
options: Jaundice with normal stool and urine colour
No itch, normal stool, dark urine
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pruritus, pale/clay-coloured stool, dark urine
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The obstructive jaundice picture comprises pruritus, pale/clay-coloured stool and dark urine.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which blood test pattern is characteristic of ascending cholangitis?
options: Normal inflammatory markers with an isolated rise in ALT
Raised WCC/CRP with obstructive LFTs (raised ALP ± GGT and bilirubin)
Raised WCC with completely normal LFTs
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Raised WCC/CRP with obstructive LFTs (raised ALP ± GGT and bilirubin)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Expect raised WCC (leucocytosis) and CRP, plus obstructive LFTs: raised ALP ± GGT and raised bilirubin.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: When should blood cultures be taken in a patient with suspected ascending cholangitis?
options: Only if blood cultures from a previous admission were negative
Only if the patient becomes hypotensive
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Before starting antibiotics
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics are started.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the first-line imaging investigation in ascending cholangitis?
options: MRCP as the first investigation in every patient with suspected cholangitis
Transabdominal ultrasound showing a dilated bile duct, with or without a visible stone
ERCP as the initial screening tool
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Transabdominal ultrasound showing a dilated bile duct, with or without a visible stone
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: USS is first-line and reliably shows bile duct dilation, though a CBD stone itself is often not seen — which is why MRCP is used when the duct is dilated or LFTs are abnormal but no stone has been found (NICE).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why is ERCP the definitive treatment in ascending cholangitis?
options: It is the only test that detects gallstones
It is the least invasive imaging method
It is non-invasive and images the tree without instrumentation
It is both diagnostic and therapeutic
It avoids any risk of pancreatitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It is both diagnostic and therapeutic
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP is the definitive treatment because it is both diagnostic and therapeutic — it is how the obstructed duct is actually decompressed. It is not the first imaging test: USS then MRCP image the tree, ERCP treats it.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: When is MRCP used in the investigation of ascending cholangitis?
options: As the definitive therapeutic intervention to relieve the obstruction
To remove stones from the common bile duct
To image the biliary tree non-invasively when USS has not shown a duct stone
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: To image the biliary tree non-invasively when USS has not shown a duct stone
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: MRCP images the biliary tree non-invasively when ultrasound has not shown duct stones but the duct is dilated and/or LFTs are abnormal (NICE). It is diagnostic only — it cannot decompress, so it never replaces ERCP.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the overarching management principle in ascending cholangitis?
options: Treat as sepsis first, then decompress the duct — antibiotics alone don't cure it
Conservative management with analgesia until the obstruction resolves
Decompress the duct first, then give antibiotics only if fever persists
Antibiotics alone are curative without decompression
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Treat as sepsis first, then decompress the duct — antibiotics alone don't cure it
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Cholangitis is a septic emergency: treat as sepsis first, then decompress the duct. Antibiotics alone don't cure it — the obstruction must be relieved.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How is the antibiotic regimen chosen in the immediate management of ascending cholangitis?
options: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per local policy, typically IV co-amoxiclav
IV gentamicin with oral metronidazole, given once the fever settles
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per local policy, typically IV co-amoxiclav
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Immediate management includes broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per local antimicrobial policy — typically IV co-amoxiclav, which already covers biliary anaerobes — given urgently, within 1 hour if high-risk sepsis criteria are met (NICE), alongside fluids, cultures and the Sepsis Six framework.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with ascending cholangitis has been resuscitated and stabilised. What is the first-line definitive treatment, and what governs its timing?
options: ERCP ± sphincterotomy + stenting, timed by severity — sooner the sicker
Long-term oral antibiotics with no drainage procedure at all
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ERCP ± sphincterotomy + stenting, timed by severity — sooner the sicker
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: After resuscitation, first-line definitive biliary decompression is ERCP ± sphincterotomy + stenting. Timing follows severity: emergency decompression if septic shock, Reynolds' pentad or failure to respond; otherwise urgently over the next day or two.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: In a patient with cholangitis where ERCP fails or is inaccessible, what is the second-line decompression option?
options: Repeat ERCP every 6 hours until successful
PTC — a radiological drain through the skin and liver
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: PTC — a radiological drain through the skin and liver
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is second-line if ERCP fails or is inaccessible — a radiological drain placed through the skin and liver.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the commonest complication of ERCP?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Acute pancreatitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The commonest complication of ERCP is acute pancreatitis; others include bleeding, perforation and repeated cholangitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which of the following correctly sequences the management of ascending cholangitis?
options: Resuscitate with fluids and IV antibiotics → urgent ERCP decompression → percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails → cholecystectomy once recovered
ERCP decompression first, then resuscitation with fluids, with antibiotics held back until after the duct has been cleared and cultures are back
PTC first → ERCP → antibiotics only if fever persists
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Resuscitate with fluids and IV antibiotics → urgent ERCP decompression → percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails → cholecystectomy once recovered
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The order is: resuscitate (fluids + IV antibiotics per local policy) → urgent ERCP decompression, sooner the sicker → percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage if ERCP fails → laparoscopic cholecystectomy once recovered, since clearing the duct alone leaves the gallstones behind.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient develops fever and jaundice two days after an ERCP performed for biliary stones. Which cause of cholangitis does this illustrate?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Iatrogenic obstruction/infection from biliary instrumentation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP/biliary instrumentation is a recognised iatrogenic cause, and recent ERCP is a classic history clue for cholangitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What fundamentally distinguishes chronic from acute pancreatitis?
options: Chronic pancreatitis produces a consistent 3× rise in serum amylase
Chronic pancreatitis is never caused by alcohol
Chronic pancreatitis causes progressive, irreversible structural and functional loss
Chronic pancreatitis never affects endocrine function
Chronic pancreatitis always resolves fully once the underlying cause is treated
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Chronic pancreatitis causes progressive, irreversible structural and functional loss
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Chronic pancreatitis is a chronic fibroinflammatory syndrome causing progressive, irreversible destruction of pancreatic parenchyma — unlike acute pancreatitis, which can fully resolve.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the defining functional consequence of chronic pancreatitis?
options: Isolated loss of endocrine function only
A reversible enzyme deficiency that recovers fully with abstinence
Loss of both exocrine function (malabsorption) and endocrine function (diabetes)
Isolated loss of exocrine function only
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Loss of both exocrine function (malabsorption) and endocrine function (diabetes)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The defining consequence is loss of both exocrine function (enzyme deficiency → malabsorption) and endocrine function (insulin deficiency → diabetes).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the single most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Chronic alcohol excess
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Chronic alcohol excess causes 70–80% of chronic pancreatitis (NICE); idiopathic is the next largest group. Smoking is strongly associated and exacerbates the disease.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which hereditary condition is a recognised cause of chronic pancreatitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: PRSS1 mutation (hereditary pancreatitis)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Hereditary causes include cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutation) and PRSS1 (hereditary pancreatitis).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A congenital cause of chronic pancreatitis in which the ducts fail to fuse, impairing drainage, is known as which of the following?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pancreas divisum
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Pancreas divisum is a congenital anomaly where the ducts fail to fuse, causing impaired drainage; annular pancreas is where the head encircles D2.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: In the obstruction-fibrosis cycle of chronic pancreatitis, what forms the imaging hallmark of the disease?
options: Calcified protein plugs forming pancreatic stones
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Calcified protein plugs forming pancreatic stones
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: In the cycle, protein-rich secretions precipitate into ductal plugs which calcify into pancreatic stones — the imaging hallmark.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why does chronic pancreatitis continue to progress even after alcohol is stopped?
options: Alcohol metabolites persist within the gland for many years afterwards
Bacterial colonisation of the duct continues
Antibodies keep attacking the acinar cells indefinitely, driving the fibrosis onward
It is a self-perpetuating cycle where each calcification worsens obstruction, damage and fibrosis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It is a self-perpetuating cycle where each calcification worsens obstruction, damage and fibrosis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The cycle is self-perpetuating: each calcification worsens obstruction → more damage → more fibrosis, so disease is irreversible even after the trigger (alcohol) is removed.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis reports epigastric pain that is reliably worse after meals. What is the mechanism?
options: Meals raise sphincter of Oddi tone via gastrin
Gastric acid directly erodes the pancreas
Food precipitates immediate ductal stone formation
Post-prandial secretin stimulates the damaged gland
Fatty food triggers CCK-driven gallbladder contraction
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Post-prandial secretin stimulates the damaged gland
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: The pain is worse after meals because, post-prandially, secretin stimulates the damaged gland.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: When do exocrine symptoms such as steatorrhoea typically appear in chronic pancreatitis?
options: Within days of the first painful episode
Once >90% of acinar cells are destroyed, often 5–25 years after pain begins
As the very first symptom, appearing long before any pain at all
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Once >90% of acinar cells are destroyed, often 5–25 years after pain begins
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Functional loss develops 5–25 years after pain; exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea, weight loss) appears once >90% of acinar cells are destroyed. Pain comes first.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which stool description is characteristic of exocrine insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis?
options: Pale stools with dark urine, pruritus and jaundice
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pale, greasy, offensive, floating stools (steatorrhoea)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Exocrine insufficiency causes steatorrhoea: pale, greasy, offensive, floating stools, with weight loss and diarrhoea.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: The diabetes of chronic pancreatitis is characteristically brittle. Why?
options: Glucagon cells are also destroyed, so there is no counter-regulation
Insulin resistance is unusually severe and progressive in these patients
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Glucagon cells are also destroyed, so there is no counter-regulation
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes is brittle and hypoglycaemia-prone because glucagon cells are also destroyed, leaving no counter-regulation.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with known chronic pancreatitis develops new-onset weight loss and worsening pain. What is the essential next step and why?
options: Re-image to exclude pancreatic carcinoma, as chronic pancreatitis raises cancer risk
Reassure the patient, as new symptoms are expected and benign in this condition
Increase the Creon dose without any further investigation at all
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Re-image to exclude pancreatic carcinoma, as chronic pancreatitis raises cancer risk
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: New-onset pain, weight loss or diabetes in known chronic pancreatitis must prompt re-imaging to exclude malignancy. Chronic pancreatitis raises pancreatic cancer risk, and the risk is highest in hereditary pancreatitis, where NICE says to consider annual monitoring.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with suspected chronic pancreatitis has a normal serum amylase. What does this indicate?
options: It points to a pancreatic abscess
It confirms an acute attack is not present
It indicates the test was performed far too early in the illness
It is consistent with chronic pancreatitis — a burnt-out gland
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It is consistent with chronic pancreatitis — a burnt-out gland
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: In chronic pancreatitis amylase/lipase are often normal or only mildly raised because the gland is burnt-out; unlike acute pancreatitis, do not expect a 3× rise.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which blood test should be sent if autoimmune pancreatitis is suspected as a cause of chronic pancreatitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: IgG4
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: IgG4 is sent if autoimmune pancreatitis is suspected.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the key functional test for exocrine insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis, and what value indicates insufficiency?
options: Amylase >3× the upper limit of normal
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Faecal elastase <200 µg/g of stool
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Faecal elastase is the key exocrine test; reduced levels <200 µg/g of stool indicate insufficiency.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the key diagnostic imaging modality in chronic pancreatitis, and its pathognomonic finding?
options: Abdominal USS showing a normal-looking pancreas
MRCP showing a chain of lakes
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: CT abdomen showing pancreatic calcification
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: CT abdomen is the key diagnostic cross-sectional test; pancreatic calcification is the pathognomonic hallmark, and it also shows ductal dilation, irregular gland outline, pseudocysts and atrophy, and excludes malignancy. Ultrasound is often the initial test but is insensitive and a normal USS does not exclude the diagnosis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: On MRCP, alternating dilated and strictured pancreatic duct produces which characteristic appearance?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Chain of lakes
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: MRI/MRCP gives better ductal detail and shows the 'chain of lakes' appearance of alternating dilated and strictured duct; it is preferred if there is no calcification on CT.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which investigation in chronic pancreatitis is both diagnostic (ductal anatomy) and therapeutic (stone removal, stenting, sphincterotomy)?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: ERCP
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: ERCP is diagnostic for ductal anatomy and therapeutic (stone removal, stenting, sphincterotomy). EUS is highly sensitive for early changes and guides biopsy.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the single most important management step in chronic pancreatitis?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Stop alcohol
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Stopping alcohol is the single most important step; it slows progression even though the damage is irreversible. Stopping smoking is recommended alongside it (NICE).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis and steatorrhoea is started on pancreatic enzyme replacement. How should Creon be taken?
options: At bedtime to cover overnight digestion
Strictly avoiding all dietary fat so that enzymes are unnecessary
With every meal and snack, titrated to symptoms
Once daily in the morning on an empty stomach
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: With every meal and snack, titrated to symptoms
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Creon is taken with every meal and snack, titrated to symptoms. Fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) levels are checked and replaced if deficient. Fat should not be restricted long term — adequate enzyme dosing is what allows a normal diet — with small frequent meals and dietitian referral.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why are long-term opioids minimised for chronic pancreatitis pain, and what is used for neuropathic-type pain instead?
options: Opioids cause hypocalcaemia; long-term NSAIDs are used
Opioids cause dependence and hyperalgesia; a neuropathic agent is used
Opioids are ineffective; coeliac plexus block is always first-line
Opioids worsen steatorrhoea; NSAIDs are first-line
Opioids are ineffective in visceral pain; paracetamol alone is used
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Opioids cause dependence and hyperalgesia; a neuropathic agent is used
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Long-term opioids cause dependence and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. For neuropathic-type pain, follow neuropathic pain guidance — amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin may each be used as the initial choice, switching if ineffective or not tolerated (NICE).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has refractory pain despite medical therapy. Which EUS-guided procedure can be used?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Coeliac plexus block
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: An EUS-guided coeliac plexus block is used for refractory pain in chronic pancreatitis.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has large ductal stones and a dilated duct (>6 mm) with head disease. Which procedure is indicated?
options: Whipple's procedure, which is reserved for suspected malignancy
Frey's procedure (local head coring + lateral pancreatojejunostomy)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Frey's procedure (local head coring + lateral pancreatojejunostomy)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Frey's procedure is indicated for large ductal stones / dilated duct (>6 mm) with head disease: local head coring + lateral pancreatojejunostomy draining the duct into a Roux-en-Y jejunal loop.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: In chronic pancreatitis, when is a Whipple's procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) preferred over a Frey's procedure?
options: When pancreatic head malignancy is suspected (resection)
When endocrine function must be preserved
When the patient has hereditary pancreatitis
When the disease is diffuse with refractory pain
When the duct contains stones needing drainage
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: When pancreatic head malignancy is suspected (resection)
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Frey's is for ductal stones (drainage); Whipple's is for suspected pancreatic head malignancy or localised head disease (resection).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient undergoes total pancreatectomy for diffuse chronic pancreatitis with refractory pain. What is the expected metabolic consequence, and what may limit it?
options: Permanent hypercalcaemia, limited by long-term bisphosphonates
Brittle diabetes; sometimes limited by autologous islet cell transplant
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Brittle diabetes; sometimes limited by autologous islet cell transplant
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Total pancreatectomy completely removes the gland → brittle diabetes; an autologous islet cell transplant is sometimes done to limit endocrine loss.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Which histological type accounts for the great majority of pancreatic cancer, and from where does it arise?
options: Exocrine adenocarcinoma arising from ductal epithelium
Neuroendocrine tumour arising from delta cells
Squamous cell carcinoma arising from acinar cells
Endocrine islet cell tumour arising from beta cells
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Exocrine adenocarcinoma arising from ductal epithelium
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Exocrine tumours are ~95% of pancreatic cancer, of which ductal adenocarcinoma is by far the commonest and the type meant by "pancreatic cancer". Neuroendocrine (islet cell) tumours are rare — under 5%.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Why do most pancreatic head tumours present earlier than tail tumours?
options: Tail tumours always cause severe pain very early in their clinical course
Head tumours produce hormones that raise the alarm far earlier on
Head tumours cause early obstructive jaundice; tail tumours are silent until advanced
Tail tumours obstruct the bile duct sooner
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Head tumours cause early obstructive jaundice; tail tumours are silent until advanced
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Most tumours arise in the head, presenting early with obstructive jaundice; body and tail tumours (20–25%) present late, being painless, silent and already advanced.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What proportion of pancreatic cancers are resectable at diagnosis?
options: The majority, because most present early
Nearly all, once staging is complete
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Only a small minority
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Only a small minority are resectable at diagnosis, because vague symptoms mean late presentation is the rule.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: What is the key modifiable risk factor for pancreatic cancer?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Smoking
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Smoking is the key modifiable risk factor, raising risk ×2–3. Age, family history and chronic pancreatitis are risk factors but not modifiable in the same way.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: How does chronic pancreatitis relate to pancreatic cancer risk?
options: It raises the risk only if alcohol is the cause
It reduces the risk by scarring the ductal epithelium
It is a recognised risk factor, highest in hereditary pancreatitis
It affects only the endocrine pancreas, so carries no cancer risk
There is no association between the two
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: It is a recognised risk factor, highest in hereditary pancreatitis
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Chronic pancreatitis is a recognised risk factor for pancreatic cancer. The risk is highest in hereditary pancreatitis, where NICE says to consider annual monitoring.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A 65-year-old presents with weight loss plus new-onset diabetes. According to NICE, what is the appropriate referral pathway?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Direct-access CT
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: NICE direct-access CT — to be performed within 2 weeks, or urgent ultrasound if CT is not available — applies to those aged 60 and over with weight loss plus any one of diarrhoea, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, or new-onset diabetes. A 2-week-wait referral is for those aged 40 and over with jaundice.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A 70-year-old presents with painless yellow sclera, pale stools, dark urine and pruritus. Which tumour location best explains this?
options: Pancreatic head compressing the common bile duct
Pancreatic body invading the coeliac plexus
A non-functional tumour with mass effect
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pancreatic head compressing the common bile duct
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Painless obstructive jaundice (yellow skin/sclera, pale stools, dark urine, pruritus) results from CBD compression by a head tumour.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: A patient with pancreatic cancer develops recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis. What is this paraneoplastic sign called?
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Trousseau's sign of malignancy
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Trousseau's sign of malignancy is recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis, a paraneoplastic hypercoagulability clue to malignancy (pancreatic, lung, other).

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: On examination a patient with painless jaundice has a palpable gallbladder. By Courvoisier's law, what does this indicate, and why?
options: Acalculous cholecystitis, because the patient is critically ill and fasting
Pancreatic/biliary malignancy, because stones cause fibrosis preventing GB distension
Gallstones, because the gallbladder is acutely inflamed
Chronic cholecystitis, because the gallbladder is shrunken
Acute cholecystitis, because the gallbladder is tender
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.answer: Pancreatic/biliary malignancy, because stones cause fibrosis preventing GB distension
conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.explanation: Courvoisier's law: painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder points to pancreatic/biliary malignancy, NOT gallstones, because stones cause scarring and fibrosis that prevent the gallbladder distending.

conditions__HEPATOBILIARY & PANCREATIC__.question: Both pancreatic cancer and cholangiocarcinoma cause painless obstructive jaundice. What primarily distinguishes them?
options: Tumour origin — biliary tree (cholangiocarcinoma) vs pancreatic head (pancreatic cancer)
Cholangiocarcinoma is always resectable at the time of diagnosis
